metadata.name: Islamism (Iranian Khomeinist tradition)
metadata.description: The Iranian Khomeinist constitutional variant: rule guided by a supreme jurist, Islamic limits on elected institutions, social obligations and national independence. This does not represent all Islamist movements or Muslims.
metadata.scope: Representative interpretation of Iran’s amended constitution and authoritative Article 44 economic policies, contextualised by Khomeini scholarship. Current UN reporting supplies explicitly distinguished implementation counterevidence; constitutional rights are not asserted to describe actual enforcement. This is one specified Islamist tradition. Neutral answers denote conditional or competing principles, including scientific causation and technology questions not settled by religious authority alone. Modern policy analogies are assessments, not fabricated statements by Khomeini.
metadata.phrase: Islamic public authority, social responsibility and national independence, with electoral institutions operating within clerical constitutional supervision.

axes.brief: Elected institutions coexist with ultimate juristic supervision, candidate vetting and leadership powers. This yields differentiated answers, not unrestricted popular sovereignty.
axes.counterEvidence: Articles 6 and 59 require elections and permit referenda; Articles 107–111 impose qualifications and removal procedures on leadership. These do not make opposition to the constitutional order equally eligible.

answers.rationale: Article 6 requires elections, but the supreme jurist and Guardian Council restrict what electoral majorities can decide.
Jurists have privileged authority under Articles 5 and 91; technical expertise alone does not establish legitimate government.
Article 6 recognises popular voting without an intelligence qualification, although eligibility and candidate choice remain regulated.
Article 110 gives leadership extraordinary policy and dispute-resolution authority above ordinary parliamentary competition.
Article 26 conditions political organisation on loyalty to Islam and the republic, excluding equal competition for every peaceful platform.
Article 76 gives parliament investigatory powers, compatible with scrutiny by representatives outside the government.
Judicial legality matters, but leadership appointments and religious review preclude the unqualified independent-court model stated.
Popular elections and juristic qualification do not confer exclusive government-selection power on trade unions.
Preservation of the Islamic republic is an explicit condition of lawful party activity under Article 26.
Article 59 permits referenda through parliamentary procedures, but popular repeal cannot displace superior Islamic constitutional requirements.
Article 110 gives leadership broad final powers while retaining parliament, government and constitutionally assigned responsibilities.
Article 111 allows removal when leadership loses qualifications; constitutional accountability is accepted through prescribed institutions.
Regular elections in Article 6 are a constitutional mechanism, not simply a personal scheduling option for the leader.
Representation and supervision both matter; citizen recall is neither necessary to juristic legitimacy nor inherently excluded for subordinate offices.
The constitutional design expressly retains elections and parliamentary accountability even while limiting their reach.
Military protection of the revolution is authorised, but independent military seizure of juristic and constitutional authority is not.

axes.brief: Public conduct is constrained by Islamic criteria alongside formal protections against arbitrary detention and intrusion.
axes.counterEvidence: The January 2026 UN communication reports allegations of lethal protest repression, arbitrary arrest and denial of counsel. These challenge constitutional guarantees; allegations are not presented as adjudicated findings.

answers.rationale: Article 4 makes Islamic criteria binding on law; adult choice alone cannot immunise prohibited intoxicant use.
Article 25 permits legally authorised interception, making a judicial serious-crime warrant compatible with the formal framework.
Article 27 protects unarmed assembly conditionally; emergency access alone does not settle the additional Islamic and public-order limits.
Article 24 excludes expression deemed detrimental to Islam, so mere offensiveness cannot guarantee protection.
Articles 3 and 29 assign public health and welfare duties beyond preventing direct injury to other people.
Article 25 protects privacy but permits statutory exceptions; the constitutional doctrine does not itself require either blanket retention or a categorical ban.
Preventing prohibited intoxication and protecting public safety justify regulated sobriety checks within this public-morality framework.
Preventive protection is accepted, but Article 32 requires lawful grounds and process; risk prediction alone does not settle detention.
Islamic limits on public culture permit restricting adult media for moral content, rather than protecting all consensual consumption.
Privacy has constitutional standing, while Islamic public-order enforcement can justify identification; neither absolute online anonymity nor universal identification follows.
Public security supports targeted emergency measures, but Article 22 and lawful-process requirements limit an unconditional suspicionless search power.
The qualified assembly protection permits restrictions where authorities judge gatherings contrary to protected public order or Islamic requirements.
Article 22 protects the home subject to law, favouring formal legal authorisation over unrestricted official entry.
Reciprocal moral scrutiny under Article 8 supports exposing wrongdoing, while confidentiality and state-security obligations qualify publication.

Article 151 requires military training while making arms possession conditional on official permission. Collective defence and regulated possession do not establish a general private self-defence entitlement from violence checks alone.
Articles 32–38 require process and forbid coerced confession; indefinite detention without court access contradicts those doctrinal safeguards despite reported abuses.

axes.brief: An Islamic national public culture coexists with recognised religious and linguistic minorities. Equal multicultural recognition remains qualified.
axes.counterEvidence: Articles 12–15 protect particular minority practices and languages; Article 19 rejects ethnic privilege. This is not a purely ethnic assimilation doctrine.

answers.rationale: Articles 12, 15 and 16 give official religious and linguistic traditions privileged public status.
Minority practices receive protection, but accommodation spending is conditional on recognition and Islamic limits rather than an unrestricted entitlement.
Public life is expected to conform to Islamic national institutions, while some minority personal practices remain protected.
Article 13 protects recognised minorities’ identity but does not establish an unconditional right to every foreign cultural practice.
Article 15 makes Persian the official language of documents and textbooks while allowing regional-language expression.
Article 19 rejects ethnic privilege, but official ceremonies also reflect Islam; inclusion depends on compatibility rather than categorical acceptance or exclusion.
The official faith and prescribed religious education favour national religious institutions in public cultural support.
Recognised distinctiveness survives within a common Islamic order rather than taking priority over it.
Article 17 prescribes the official calendar and Friday holiday, supporting a shared public calendar.
Multiple recognised traditions have a place, but they do not displace Islam’s constitutionally superior defining role.
National unity under Article 9 supports integration into shared institutions while leaving lawful minority practices intact.

Official Persian supports a common public language, while public signs in additional languages can serve practical access. The constitutional language settlement does not require either universal multilingual signage or a blanket prohibition.
Family and educational institutions transmit the shared Islamic public identity, qualified by minority personal-law protections.
Religious covering has a privileged moral justification within Islamic public life, though identity and security rules could still impose exceptions.
Article 13 accepts several recognised communities’ ways of life within limits rather than equal acceptance of every lifestyle.
Integration entails conformity with Islamic public rules without necessarily abandoning every regional custom.

axes.brief: Islamic solidarity and asylum coexist with sovereign admission control and citizen-focused social duties.
axes.counterEvidence: UNHCR records 197,300 deportations among 249,100 returns to Afghanistan in early 2026. This is implementation evidence against equating shared Muslim identity with unrestricted admission, not a universal Islamist prescription.

answers.rationale: Sovereign border control and resource duties permit annual limits, although Islamic solidarity can justify exceptions.
Work and dignity matter, but Article 42 leaves foreigners’ admission and citizenship subject to law rather than an unconditional migration right.
Economic needs support skilled admission, while asylum and Islamic solidarity supply non-economic grounds against a skills-only rule.
Article 10 values family stability, but family unity does not automatically override sovereign admission conditions.
Article 155 permits asylum with exclusions; humanitarian protection and political-security criteria prevent an unconditional permanent-residence commitment.
The regulated admission framework and documented deportations weigh against a general entitlement to remain after unlawful entry.
Labour demand is one consideration within sovereign national planning, not an automatic exception to immigration controls.
Constitutional housing and citizen-welfare responsibilities provide grounds for reducing admission under severe capacity pressures.
Family protection supports reunion, but resource planning permits limits; the doctrine does not make either interest universally decisive.
Useful employment favours admission, qualified by national law, security and social capacity rather than an unrestricted job-offer entitlement.
Sponsorship can secure support, but asylum and broader Islamic solidarity provide legitimate admissions without employer sponsorship.
Education can support integration and skills, but graduation neither guarantees residence nor doctrinally excludes a lawful route to it.
Article 155 supports asylum while retaining political exclusions; emergency protection can warrant flexibility without a general cap override.
Shared Islamic public norms favour cultural compatibility, though recognised minorities and non-ethnic equality qualify this preference.
Social welfare is framed primarily around citizens, while dignity and assistance can extend to foreigners; equal immediate entitlement is not prescribed.
Admission serves national and religious responsibilities, not cultural diversity as an independent selection priority.

axes.brief: Independence, armed protection of the revolution and defence of Muslims coexist with formal non-domination and peaceful relations.
axes.counterEvidence: Articles 152–154 reject domination and invoke noninterference. Revolutionary solidarity may nevertheless support action beyond territorial self-defence; no specific 2026 military event is inferred here.

answers.rationale: Protecting independence and Muslims can justify action beyond a prior attack, while Article 152 rejects domination for ordinary national advantage.
Peaceful relations with non-belligerent states support trying diplomacy where compatible with independence and religious obligations.
Articles 144–151 prioritise capable revolutionary defence, allowing substantial expenditure without prescribing unlimited military superiority.
Preventing an imminent attack fits the constitutional duty to preserve independence even before an attack lands.
Defence of Muslims and support for just struggles are broader than responding only after the country itself is attacked.
Article 151 requires military training for citizens, supporting compulsory defence obligations rather than a wholly voluntary force.
Peaceful relations support compromise, but independence and revolutionary commitments limit concessions to avoid conflict.
Defence effectiveness and Islamic responsibility both apply; neither autonomous weapons adoption nor blanket rejection follows without reliability and legal judgement.
Article 154 solidarity is not confined to domestic territorial defence, allowing some outward support.
Avoiding war at any cost would subordinate obligations to Muslims and national independence to an absolute peace rule.
External commitments can serve revolutionary aims, but non-domination and national needs qualify an open-ended expeditionary commitment.
Peace matters, yet Article 9 makes territorial integrity fundamental; an unresolved dispute cannot always be preferred to defensive force.
Deterrence may protect independence, while coercive domination is rejected; the purpose of the threat determines the judgement.
Safeguarding independence can warrant accepting a risk of war rather than conceding to external pressure; reducing war risk therefore does not invariably take priority over demonstrating resolve.
Security duties can justify necessary foreign intelligence collection, subject to leadership judgement and religious constraints.
Agreed restraint can serve peace, but disarmament cannot compromise the armed capacity required to defend the republic.

axes.brief: National sovereignty and resistance to foreign domination strongly constrain binding international authority. Islamic solidarity remains transnational.
axes.counterEvidence: Article 11 seeks Muslim political unity and Article 154 supports struggles abroad; these qualify purely inward nationalism without granting secular international institutions final authority.

answers.rationale: Articles 4 and 153 reserve law to Islamic constitutional authority and reject agreements establishing foreign control.
International cooperation is possible, but outside binding authority cannot override religious law and national independence.
Domestic Islamic judicial authority takes precedence over external adjudication imposed contrary to national constitutional principles.
Alliance obligations are conditional on independence and cannot unconditionally bind the state to outside decisions.
Retaining sovereignty requires a way to reject arrangements that become instruments of foreign control.
International courts may facilitate agreement but cannot hold unquestioned supremacy over Islamic constitutional law.
National independence is central, yet obligations to Muslims and oppressed peoples sometimes reach beyond narrow national advantage.
Article 50 supports environmental protection without transferring final coercive authority to an external institution.
Article 152’s nonalignment principle favours an independent foreign policy over compulsory bloc positions.
External human-rights interpretation cannot overrule the Islamic criteria made supreme by Article 4.
Economic independence and protection against foreign domination favour sovereign monetary control.
Joint funding can express Islamic cooperation, but externally imposed allocations compromising independence would be rejected.
Control of admission and national territory belongs to the sovereign republic under Articles 9 and 42.
Cooperative trade is permissible under Article 44 policy, but common rules remain conditional on independence and Islamic law.
A secular federation overriding Iran is inconsistent with sovereignty, while Article 11 positively envisages Muslim political unity.
A global rule is not binding merely because it is globally beneficial when it conflicts with Islamic-national constitutional obligations.

axes.brief: The amended economic model combines private and cooperative enterprise with public strategic networks and welfare obligations.
axes.counterEvidence: Original Article 44 was much more publicly owned; the later general policies authorise broad privatisation. Providing a service as a public duty does not necessarily mean owning every provider.

answers.rationale: Article 44 implementation encourages private and cooperative activity across ordinary commerce while reserving strategic sectors.
Essential natural resources and network functions fit public stewardship, although delivery arrangements can involve non-state providers.
The revised policy favours expanding non-state provision where performance is equivalent and reserved functions are unaffected.
Competitive enterprises may be sold under Article 44 policy; state ownership remains justified for strategic tasks rather than all competition.
Article 29 requires health access, but the mixed economy does not require either predominantly private or exclusively public provision.
Privatisation policy permits non-state rail businesses while strategic infrastructure can remain publicly controlled.
Efficient non-state provision fits the government’s revised supervisory role where Islamic and service obligations remain enforceable.
Article 44 policies permit non-government banks while reserving named banks to the state. This specifically supports public banks operating alongside private banks.
Authorised transfer of many commercial shares supports sales where firms are outside reserved strategic functions.
Article 31 requires housing provision, particularly for those in need, but ownership can be public, cooperative or private.
Defence and security activities are expressly excluded from broad privatisation, outweighing a general private-provider preference.
Article 45 and retained oil and gas extraction establish strong public control over natural-resource wealth.
Non-strategic municipal delivery may be contracted within the expanding non-state sector, provided public obligations survive.
Article 44 policies retain specified strategic energy, communications and defence functions under public control.
Losses can justify restructuring or transfer, but strategic reserves and employment duties can justify continued public ownership.
Article 175 and Article 44 exclusions preserve state broadcasting rather than making its public ownership incidental.

axes.brief: Economic self-sufficiency and protection from domination qualify permission for trade and non-state enterprise.
axes.counterEvidence: The Article 44 policies seek gradual interaction with international trade, so autarky and a ban on every foreign investment are not implied.

answers.rationale: Article 43’s self-sufficiency and employment aims support protective tariffs when necessary for national production.
Removing all barriers would forfeit tools used to prevent dependence and support strategic domestic capacity.
Domestic sourcing can justify higher costs when it sustains economic independence rather than merely maximising cheap imports.
Cheapest global supply is not decisive where it creates strategic dependence prohibited by the constitutional economic framework.
Articles 43 and 153 support restrictions protecting essential supplies against foreign domination.
Unilateral liberalisation is conditional on domestic capacity and independence, not a general obligation regardless of partners.
Developing national productive capability can warrant temporary infant-industry protection under Article 43.
Foreign investment cannot claim unconditional equality where strategic control and independence are at stake.
Food-production self-sufficiency provides a reason to restrict agricultural imports despite consumer-price advantages.
Trade integration encourages adjustment, while employment and independence justify protection; no universal adjustment-only rule follows.
Countermeasures can defend economic independence against discriminatory foreign restrictions, subject to national-interest judgement.
Equal product taxation can facilitate commerce, but origin-based strategic measures remain legitimate under independence priorities.
Restrictions against subsidised imports can protect national production from externally supported dependence.
Deliberately increasing dependence conflicts with Article 43’s stated self-sufficiency objective.
Agreements conferring foreign control over strategic resources or institutions conflict directly with Article 153.
Digital commerce can contribute to trade, but Islamic cultural rules and security concerns qualify unrestricted cross-border access.

axes.brief: Private initiative operates within strategic plans, Islamic commercial rules and social guarantees.
axes.counterEvidence: Privatisation expands decision-making outside government, while Article 43 explicitly rejects making the state the sole employer. Planning is substantial but not total allocation of every output.

answers.rationale: Private enterprises have room to decide output, qualified by national planning and Islamic economic restrictions.
Strategic production targets can advance Article 43 self-sufficiency without requiring quotas for every small business.
Market pricing is compatible with non-state enterprise, but anti-exploitation and essential-needs obligations permit intervention.
Constitutional economic planning and Article 44 supervisory functions support directing investment toward national priorities.
Consumer preferences matter within markets but cannot displace collective requirements for independence and basic needs.
Anti-exploitation and guaranteed necessities justify controlling essential prices where ordinary markets frustrate those duties.
Occupational freedom supports entry, but national planning and Islamic legality can justify conditions beyond private willingness.
The retained public banks and strategic supervisory role permit directing credit toward development priorities.
Capital movement can be restricted where it undermines independence, financing priorities or lawful Islamic transactions.
Targeted support to cooperatives, poorer groups and productive development is explicitly part of the Article 44 framework.
Independent private currencies would be conditional on national monetary and Islamic commercial supervision, not an unrestricted market right.
Preventing exploitation and ensuring livelihoods support wage floors, although the doctrine does not specify their level.
Negotiation is legitimate but bounded by labour protections and social planning rather than an exclusive wage-setting principle.
Public monetary institutions can serve national economic priorities while remaining constrained by Islamic finance rules.
Housing as a constitutional need justifies intervention rather than leaving rents entirely to market allocation.
Article 43 calls for coordinated economic planning, qualified by private and cooperative activity rather than complete administrative control.

axes.brief: Poverty removal, broad social insurance and protection against concentration accompany recognition of legitimate private wealth.
axes.counterEvidence: Articles 46–47 protect earnings and lawful property; Article 49 targets illicit wealth, not every fortune. Exact tax rates and benefit durations remain policy choices.

answers.rationale: Article 43 opposes concentrated wealth and poverty, supporting taxation that reduces materially harmful income gaps.
Large differences can be grounds for intervention when associated with exploitation or concentration, beyond absolute deprivation alone.

Article 29 requires comprehensive social support. A stronger minimum income floor is a defensible application of that obligation, with higher contributions justified to fund it within the constitution’s economic constraints.
Articles 29–31 promise social security, education and housing beyond a narrowly subsistence-only safety net.
Progressive contributions fit the combined social-duty and property framework without requiring confiscation of all higher earnings.
Keeping more wealth is qualified by obligations to finance common welfare and prevent exploitative concentration.
Inherited property and family obligations are recognised within Islamic law; additional inheritance taxation depends on lawful design and social need.
Article 29 recognises unemployment protection as a right rather than conditioning all working-age support on a fixed expiry.
Wealth concentration may justify taxation, but legitimate holdings receive protection; a general annual wealth tax is not doctrinally mandatory.
Low taxes cannot automatically take priority over the constitutional commitment to comprehensive social protection.
Article 43 includes time and opportunity for intellectual, social and political development beyond bare physical survival.
Tax reduction is subordinate to meeting welfare duties where it would undermine guaranteed provision.
Support for workers unable to meet basic needs fits Article 43’s employment and livelihood responsibilities.
A flat marginal rate has no privileged status where social financing and differing capacity justify progressive contributions.
Housing and anti-concentration goals support some land reform, but legitimate property and the terms of compensation require case-specific judgement.
Limiting all benefits to minimal necessities conflicts with the broader social insurance and educational rights enumerated constitutionally.

axes.brief: Islamic legal supremacy and formal clerical supervision are constitutive of this variant.
axes.counterEvidence: Recognised religious minorities retain specified rites and personal-law protections. These coexist with official Shiism and do not amount to secular equal separation.

answers.rationale: Article 4 expressly requires laws to conform to Islamic criteria, rejecting religion-free public legislation.
Islamic sources have binding legislative authority rather than serving only as private ethical inspiration.
Clerical Guardian Council review is constitutionally required for legislation’s Islamic compatibility.
Article 12 makes Twelver Ja'fari Islam the official and unalterable religion.
Articles 16 and 30 place education within an Islamic constitutional order rather than a religiously neutral curriculum.
The state’s Islamic mission supports formal religious teaching as part of public education.
Courts are state institutions, but their authority is constrained by religious law and recognised religious personal-law rules.
Articles 91–96 establish clerical scrutiny of parliamentary laws for compatibility with Islam.
Official religious observance is compatible with, and expressive of, the constitutional Islamic state.
Supporting Islamic institutions follows the official religious and educational functions of government.
An official Islamic constitutional identity permits religious symbolism in public institutions.
Article 17 specifies the Islamic calendar and Friday as the official weekly holiday.
Religious qualification directly determines eligibility for the supreme leadership and clerical Guardian Council positions.

Article 51 places taxation and exemptions under law, itself subject to Islamic requirements. Religious obligations and public support do not by themselves establish a general special tax exemption for religious organisations.
Article 10 places family arrangements under Islamic law, rejecting removal of religious requirements merely for secular uniformity.
Articles 12–13 recognise religious personal-law arrangements alongside the state’s overarching Islamic judiciary.

axes.brief: The family and public morality are defined through Islamic criteria rather than individual revision of inherited moral rules.
axes.counterEvidence: Constitutional education, work and public participation for women coexist with differentiated family roles. The profile does not equate all change or all female employment with prohibited conduct.

answers.rationale: Custom can change where compatible with Islam, but individual preference alone does not override binding religious moral norms.
Article 10 protects family sanctity and stability within Islamic ethics, favouring continuity in public moral institutions.
Equal recognition of every household form conflicts with the prescribed Islamic family framework.
Article 21’s maternal and family provisions support differentiated responsibilities while also acknowledging women’s social rights.
Marriage recognition is governed by the Islamic family framework, which does not imply recognition of same-sex marriage.
Article 10 treats the established family as society’s foundational unit deserving special protection.
Personal social preference alone is insufficient to justify abortion within a religiously governed family and life-protection framework.
Religious upbringing and family authority support parental objections to conflicting teaching, qualified by the state’s Islamic curriculum.
The prescribed marriage and family structure conflicts with an equal entitlement to adoption by same-sex couples.
Public moral duties under Article 8 support requirements for religiously defined modest conduct and dress.
Language changes based solely on self-defined identity are conditional on compatibility with established religious sex and family categories.
The constitutional supremacy of Islamic criteria gives established religious morality priority over unrestricted lifestyle experimentation.
Work and public participation for women are recognised, while family roles remain differentiated; crossing a conventional role is judged by its specific religious compatibility.
Changes to social institutions must preserve Islamic and family obligations, supporting caution about unrestricted transformation.

Teaching information about sexual orientations and gender identities can coexist with a religious curriculum that rejects equal moral approval. The question asks about teaching the topics, so religious family norms alone do not settle the permissibility of descriptive instruction.
Inherited custom is protected when compatible with Islam, but ancestry alone cannot legitimate a practice contrary to religious law.

axes.brief: Scientific development is valued alongside public health, Islamic ethical review and unusually explicit constitutional environmental duties.
axes.counterEvidence: Article 43 encourages technical capability; Article 50 forbids irreparable environmental damage. Modern biotechnology and AI examples are conditional analogies, not historical doctrinal pronouncements.

answers.rationale: Article 43 values new technical capacity, but health, environment and Islamic legality can justify delaying specific products.
Protecting health under Article 29 supports supervised trials when safety is materially uncertain.
Article 50’s prohibition of irreparable environmental damage weighs against infrastructure justified solely by economic growth.
Medical progress is valued, but social health duties support evidence requirements before exposing the public to uncertain lasting harm.
Productivity and technical independence favour AI, while Article 43’s employment duty gives displacement independent weight.
Environmental protection is a public duty to future generations, supporting preservation despite some foregone construction.
Food security supports novel production, but religious permissibility and health assessment can change the decision on cultivated meat.
Uncertain invasive brain procedures implicate health and ethical obligations, supporting controlled trials before broad availability.
Technology can advance self-sufficiency, while Article 43 also rejects waste; neither technological substitution nor consumption restraint always takes priority.
Credible unresolved environmental harm warrants delay under Article 50 even when development has economic benefits.
Adult choice matters, but basic safety alone need not resolve religious, health and social concerns about elective brain enhancement.
The constitutional health duty supports testing diagnostic reliability before routine medical deployment.
Scientific capability is valued, but hereditary enhancement requires specific religious and medical judgement beyond a blanket permission or prohibition.
Food security does not remove the environmental and health grounds for longer-term assessment of modified crops.
Article 31 housing duties and Article 50 environmental duties must be reconciled; neither automatically overrides all remaining land protection.
Article 50 expressly opposes irreparable environmental damage, supporting delay when such harm remains a credible possibility.

axes.brief: Local elected councils operate within a centrally sovereign Islamic republic.
axes.counterEvidence: Articles 100–106 give councils actual constitutional functions and safeguards against arbitrary dissolution; these remain subordinate to Islamic and national law.

answers.rationale: Articles 100–106 constitutionally recognise elected local councils, giving local authority more than a purely discretionary administrative basis.
Article 105 requires council decisions to comply with Islamic criteria and national law.
Article 9 protects territorial integrity, precluding a unilateral regional right to secede by local vote.
National authorities can override local decisions that breach national or Islamic requirements, though lawful local jurisdiction is recognised.
Local councils operate under the national constitution rather than independent regional constitutional sovereignty.
Central responsibility for security and revolutionary protection favours national policing authority alongside local administration.
Article 48 balances regional resources and needs; local revenue interests coexist with national equitable allocation.
Articles 15–16 prescribe national language and religious educational requirements rather than leaving curricula wholly regional.
Councils have lawful local functions, but tax authority depends on national legislation rather than inherent regional fiscal sovereignty.
Article 43’s economic and employment duties support national standards across local jurisdictions.
Local boundaries remain within centrally protected territorial and administrative sovereignty, not autonomous municipal choice alone.
Article 29 defines a nationwide social-security and health responsibility applicable beyond regional discretion.
Ethnic and linguistic equality supports cultural rights, while Article 9 and national law limit separate Indigenous territorial sovereignty.
National equity under Article 48 can justify limiting competition that undermines shared revenues and regional development.
Local councils can manage local concerns, but Article 50’s environmental duty permits overriding national protective standards.
Military assistance and coordinated state responsibility support central action in national disasters under Article 147.

axes.brief: Moral education, family formation and spiritual agency are important, but these do not constitute a scientific theory of every measured trait.
axes.counterEvidence: Khomeini’s spiritual conception of human development is neither genetic determinism nor a claim that biology is irrelevant. Neutral causal answers register this substantive non-reductionism, not a covert empirical conclusion.

answers.rationale: The constitutional educational mission and moral cultivation assign upbringing substantial influence on behaviour without denying bodily dispositions.

Spiritual and educational formation matter in this tradition, but neither those commitments nor constitutional equality settles the relative biological and social causes of average intelligence differences between countries.
Differentiated family roles and education both matter, leaving the relative causal contribution of socialisation and biology unresolved within the model.
Spiritual discipline can reshape responses while humans remain embodied; religious doctrine does not prescribe a predominantly biological account of stress variation.
The emphasis on education and cultivated capacities supports experience as a substantial influence on interests.
Moral responsibility and personal formation coexist with bodily dispositions; no general hereditary primacy for risk-taking is implied.
Article 8’s reciprocal moral obligations and education aim to cultivate cooperation through social practice.
Religious duties to others can develop empathy, but the doctrine does not rank that development above or below all biological differences.
Education matters to attention, yet the constitutional educational duty does not establish a comparative neurodevelopmental causal claim.
The doctrine treats moral capacities through spiritual nature and cultivation, not a simple biological-versus-social predominance.
Learning and moral interpretation shape perceived danger without establishing that inherited defensive responses are generally secondary.
Individual disposition and spiritual self-development coexist; a constitutional religious programme does not settle temperament heritability.

Religious moral education and embodied human capacities both enter this account of persons; the sources do not rank cultural learning against biology as the main influence on preferences about physical attractiveness.

Moral accountability and social formation coexist with recognition of embodied capacities. Neither constitutional ethnic equality nor religious duty establishes that biological racial differences are the main cause of group differences in violent behaviour.
Education and moral self-discipline are meaningful routes to self-control, rather than a fixed racial inheritance account.
Differentiated family duties and economic organisation both affect pay, so the doctrine does not reduce observed gaps to either market value or norms alone.

review.reviewer: Codex /root, separate evidence review of /root/libertarian_historical assessment
review.notes: Independently read all 240 answers against the current question wording and checked the constitution, Article 44 policies, Iranica scholarship, January 2026 UN communication and May 2026 UNHCR return data. Corrected the war-risk agreement direction and mixed public/private banking answer. Distinguished regulated arms possession from a general private entitlement, descriptive teaching from moral approval, religious obligations from tax exemptions, and moral equality from empirical causal claims. Corrected public-signage and physical-attractiveness interpretations. Constitutional rights remain formal commitments; recent UN reporting is separately attributed implementation counterevidence, including allegations rather than adjudicated findings. Neutral answers explicitly preserve conditional or non-ranking interpretations; this specified Iranian tradition does not represent all Islamism or Muslims.
